endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: Ultimately, the output of the combination of radiologist plus the AI system must be optimized.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: CDRH notes that for GenAI-enabled functions involving care escalation decisions, such as advising whether to seek emergency care, both under-escalation and over-escalation can impact assessment of risk of such functions.

endorsements.title: Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care Medicine: a consensus of 22
endorsements.quote: The first step toward integration is to understand how clinicians interact with AI and to design systems that complement, rather than disrupt, clinical reasoning [ 32 ].

endorsements.title: A perspective for adapting generalist AI to specialized medical AI applications and their challenges
endorsements.quote: Furthermore, real-world user studies serve as the gold standard for evaluation.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing machine-assisted translation in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Success should be defined by practical outcomes, such as faster translation turnaround times, higher user satisfaction (both for translators and patients), and improved patient outcomes, rather than technical metrics alone.

endorsements.title: Bridging innovation and clinical reality: Interpreting the comparative study of deep learning models for multi-class upper gastrointestinal disease segmentation
endorsements.quote: The observational experiments for human-AI interaction trials should be applied that endoscopists use model outputs in a simulated or live environment to measure behavioral changes.

endorsements.title: Prioritizing human-AI collaboration in healthcare: the TRIAD framework for trustworthy governance, real-world, and integrated adaptive deployment
endorsements.quote: This framework evaluates the human-AI team in real workflows using team-level metrics, including accuracy, safety, workload, and patterns of acceptance, editing, and overriding.

endorsements.title: Trustworthy AI-Augmented Objective Structured Clinical Examinations in Nursing Education: Taiwan-Japan Viewpoint on 5 AI Roles, Governance, and Cross-Border Implementation
endorsements.quote: Mock OSCEs introduce AI‑assisted stations and compare conditions with and without AI support to quantify benefits and harms in context.

endorsements.title: Rethinking scale in ophthalmic artificial intelligence: from bigger models to smarter clinical reasoning
endorsements.quote: Such paradigms may also need to include clinically weighted error analysis, uncertainty quantification, longitudinal consistency, and human-AI interaction studies that assess decision-support quality rather than prediction accuracy alone.

endorsements.title: A six-level clinical autonomy framework for artificial intelligence in dentistry
endorsements.quote: Beyond diagnostic accuracy, evaluation should incorporate human–AI interaction metrics, including decision latency, trust calibration, and susceptibility to automation bias.

endorsements.title: Knowledge Engine, Wisdom System: Aligning Generative AI With the Relational and Epistemic Foundations of Primary Care
endorsements.quote: Technical performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall are necessary but not enough.

endorsements.title: From Algorithm to Bedside: A Clinician's Framework for AI in Practice
endorsements.quote: Local workflow evaluation, both before and after deployment, should map who will use the tool, when they will see it, how they will act, what competing tasks they face, and what happens to patients who do or do not receive the AI-triggered intervention.

endorsements.title: The Cognitive Transaction: Toward a Human Factors Research Agenda for AI in Anesthesia and Perioperative Care
endorsements.quote: Evaluating the cognitive transaction under perioperative conditions, not the computational model in isolation, is both a methodological imperative and a patient safety priority.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Automated Echocardiographic Analysis and the Workflow of Sonographers: A Randomized Crossover Trial (AI-Echo RCT)
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Heart Association
evidence.outcome: AI performance as used by sonographers in the intended workflow, including effects on user performance
evidence.effect: AI assistance shortened exam time, increased daily exams and parameters analyzed (85±12 vs 25±1); AI values agreed with expert-endorsed values within limits for 90% of parameters.
evidence.quote: This real-world randomized trial demonstrated that AI-based echocardiographic analysis enhances workflow efficiency, reduces sonographer fatigue, and improves image quality without compromising diagnostic integrity.

evidence.title: Interval cancer, sensitivity, and specificity comparing AI-supported mammography screening with standard double reading without AI in the MASAI study: a randomised, controlled, non-inferiority, single-blinded, population-based, screening-accuracy trial
evidence.outcome: screening sensitivity
evidence.effect: Sensitivity was higher in the intervention group (80.5%) than the control group (73.8%).
evidence.quote: Sensitivity was higher in the intervention group (80·5% [95% CI 76·4-84·2]) than the control group (73·8% [68·9-78·3]; p=0·031), an effect consistent across age and breast density, and for invasive cancer but not for in-situ cancer.

evidence.title: Evaluating real-world deployment of an HL7-CDA-aligned LLM for ICD-10-CM coding
evidence.outcome: Coding time with AI-assisted versus manual workflows
evidence.effect: Across 10,688 coded summaries, all three AI-assisted workflows were faster than manual coding (Games-Howell, all p < 0.001). PubMedGPT-2 produced the largest average time reduction, followed by BioMistral and HAN.
evidence.quote: All three AI-assisted workflows yielded faster completion times than manual coding (Games-Howell, all p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: discharge summaries coded in RCT (10 certified coding specialists)

evidence.title: Developing and Validating a Prediction Model For Death or Critical Illness in Hospitalized Adults, an Opportunity for Human-Computer Collaboration
evidence.outcome: Combined human-plus-model prediction sensitivity versus clinicians alone or model alone
evidence.effect: Combined predictions detected 49% of deterioration events, improving sensitivity by 16% vs clinicians alone and 24% vs model alone, with PPV of 33%.
evidence.quote: Combining human and model predictions detected 49% of clinical deterioration events, improving sensitivity by 16% compared with clinicians alone and 24% compared with the model alone while maintaining a positive predictive value of 33%, thus keeping false alarms at a clinically acceptable level.

evidence.title: Prospective implementation of AI-assisted screen reading to improve early detection of breast cancer
evidence.outcome: Cancer detection, recalls, predictive value, and reading workload in the human–AI workflow
evidence.effect: Compared with double reading, AI-assisted reading added 0.7-1.6 cancers per 1,000 cases, 0.16-0.30% recalls and 4-6% overall reading workload; PPV increased 0.1-1.9%.
evidence.quote: The results showed that, compared to double reading, implementing the AI-assisted additional-reader process could achieve 0.7-1.6 additional cancer detection per 1,000 cases, with 0.16-0.30% additional recalls, 0-0.23% unnecessary recalls and a 0.1-1.9% increase in positive predictive value (PPV) after 7-11% additional human reads of AI-flagged cases (equating to 4-6% additional overall reading workload).

evidence.title: Impact of real-life use of artificial intelligence as support for human reading in a population-based breast cancer screening program with mammography and tomosynthesis
evidence.outcome: Cancer detection rate, recall rate, and positive predictive value of recalls
evidence.effect: With versus without AI: CDR 9.0‰ vs 5.8‰; PPV 14.6% vs 10.6%; recall rate 6.1% vs 5.4% (all p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: The implementation of an AI system for concurrent decision support for reading DM and DBT screening exams increased the breast cancer detection rate (CDR) by 3.2‰ (9.0‰ vs 5.8‰; p < 0.001) and the positive predictive value (PPV) of the recalled women by 4% (14.6% vs 10.6%; p < 0.001) with an acceptable increase in recall rate (RR) by 0.7% (6.1% vs 5.4%; p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: women (screening examinations; 11,998 AI-supported and 11,998 matched historical controls)

evidence.title: Prospective Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage of Incidental Pulmonary Emboli on Contrast-Enhanced CT Examinations of the Chest or Abdomen
evidence.outcome: diagnostic performance
evidence.effect: Sensitivity was 80.0% without AI vs 96.2% with AI (p=.03), with no significant difference in specificity.
evidence.quote: Radiologists without AI, in comparison to radiologists with AI, showed significantly lower sensitivity (80.0% vs 96.2%, respectively; p = .03), without a significant difference in specificity (99.9% vs 99.9%, p = .58), for the detection of IPE.

evidence.title: Prospective Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage of Intracranial Hemorrhage on Noncontrast Head CT Examinations
evidence.outcome: Radiologist diagnostic performance and ICH-positive report turnaround with versus without AI.
evidence.effect: Without versus with AI: accuracy 99.5% vs 99.2%; sensitivity 98.6% vs 98.9%; specificity 99.8% vs 99.3% (p = .004); mean report turnaround 147.1 minutes versus 149.9 minutes (p = .11).
evidence.quote: An AI triage system for ICH detection did not improve radiologists' diagnostic performance or report turnaround times.

evidence.title: Implementation and clinical evaluation of an in-house thoracic auto-segmentation model for 0.35 T magnetic resonance imaging guided radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Correlation of standalone geometric metrics with clinician correction times
evidence.effect: Weak to negligible Spearman correlations between geometric metrics and correction times for most OARs; significant only for aorta, esophagus, left lung. Time savings could not be predicted from geometric metrics.
evidence.quote: Time saving potential could not be estimated from model geometric performance metrics.

evidence.title: Real-world clinical impact of three commercial AI algorithms on musculoskeletal radiography interpretation: A prospective crossover reader study
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in intended workflow versus unaided reading
evidence.effect: Diagnostic AUCs unchanged with AI; median interpretation times decreased (Reader 1: 34 s to 21-25 s; Reader 2: 30 s to 21-26 s; p < 0.001); confidence improved.
evidence.quote: Median interpretation times decreased with AI (Reader 1: 34 s to 21-25 s; Reader 2: 30 s to 21-26 s; all p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: adult musculoskeletal studies (2,926 radiographs) read by 2 radiologists

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence in Colonoscopy: A Tool, Not a Necessity for Experts
evidence.outcome: Endoscopist detection performance with AI in intended workflow versus without AI
evidence.effect: No significant improvement in ADR (35% vs 31%, p=0.2) or PDR (42% vs 38%, p=0.22) for experienced endoscopist; withdrawal time significantly shorter with AI (9.34 vs 10.44 min; p<0.0001).
evidence.quote: AIAC may not significantly improve adenoma or PDRs when performed by an experienced endoscopist.

evidence.title: Exploring the influence of endoscopist characteristics and artificial intelligence on adenoma detection in colonoscopy
evidence.outcome: Adenoma detection rate with vs without AI assistance by endoscopist sex, in real workflow
evidence.effect: AI improved ADR among male endoscopists (AOR 1.166, 95% CI 1.064 to 1.278; p = 0.001) but had no significant effect for females; male ADR rose to 28.77% vs female without AI 30.05%.
evidence.quote: AI assistance improved ADR among male endoscopists (AOR 1.166, 95% CI 1.064 to 1.278; p = 0.001) but had no significant effect for females.

evidence.title: Evaluation of computer-aided detection for gastric cancer using white-light and linked-color imaging: a pilot study
evidence.outcome: Gastric cancer detection by endoscopists with versus without CADe
evidence.effect: Detection was 4.8% with CADe versus 0.95% in matched controls; absolute difference 3.85% (95% CI, 0.67%-8.29%; P = .098), reported as not statistically significant.
evidence.quote: After matching, 1 GC was detected among 105 patients in the control group (0.95%), with an absolute difference of 3.85% (95% CI, 0.67%-8.29%; P = .098).

evidence.title: Computer-Aided Colonoscopy Alert Fatigue and Its Effect on Adenoma Detection
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in real workflow versus without, across the day
evidence.effect: Adenomas per colonoscopy rose +0.27 (95% CI 0.14-0.41) early with CADe but only +0.11 (95% CI -0.09 to 0.31, P=0.51) later.
evidence.quote: Similarly, adenomas per colonoscopy were significantly higher in early CADe-assisted procedures (mean increase +0.27, 95% CI [0.14-0.41], P < 0.001), but this benefit disappeared in later procedures (+0.11, 95% CI [-0.09 to 0.31], P = 0.51).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-based smartphone application for skin cancer detection: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study
evidence.outcome: diagnostic accuracy of combined human-AI team
evidence.effect: Adding teledermatology review to the AI output increased specificity to 86.8% but resulted in a lower sensitivity of 75.3% compared to standalone metrics.
evidence.quote: Combined CNN and teledermatology review resulted in increased specificity (86.8%; P < 0.001), with a sensitivity of 75.3%.

evidence.title: Hybrid supervised deep learning for lung adenocarcinoma diagnosis to optimize surgical strategies
evidence.outcome: manual diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: manual diagnostic accuracy improved by 22.9%
evidence.quote: With its assistance, manual diagnostic accuracy improved by 22.9% ( n = 3, 11.7%, 28.5%, 28.5%).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Chest Radiography: A Prospective Crossover Multi-Reader Study on Diagnostic Performance and Workflow Efficiency
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in the intended workflow versus without AI
evidence.effect: No improvement in diagnostic accuracy with AI; accuracy decreased in several reader-tool pairings for effusions and nodules through increased false positives.
evidence.quote: For pleural effusions and pulmonary nodules, accuracy decreased in several reader-tool pairings due to increased false positives.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (1861 radiographs) read by five readers

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence guided physician directive improves head and neck planning quality and practice Uniformity: A prospective study
evidence.outcome: Radiotherapy plan achievability, quality, and planning efficiency with versus without AI-guided physician directives
evidence.effect: Achievability increased from 52.9% to 80.4%; first-plan acceptance improved from 63.3% to 90%; maximum iterations decreased from 4 to 2; four organs-at-risk had statistically significant dose reductions (range 4.3 to 15.2 Gy).
evidence.quote: As seen in Fig. 4 a, there is a significant increase in plan achievability pre- and post-AI guidance, from 52.9% to 80.4%.

evidence.title: Deep learning and atlas-based models to streamline the segmentation workflow of total marrow and lymphoid irradiation
evidence.outcome: DSC for CTV_LN delineation
evidence.effect: Median DSC increased from 0.70 with the standalone model to 0.94 after manual revision.
evidence.quote: The AB model achieved a median DSC of 0.70 [0.66;0.74] for CTV_LN delineation, increasing to 0.94 [0.94;0.95] after manual revision, with minimal Dmean differences.

evidence.title: Validation and three years of clinical experience in using an artificial intelligence algorithm as a second read system for prostate cancer diagnosis-real-world experience
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic revisions following AI-assisted second review in routine pathology workflow
evidence.effect: Over 3 years, diagnoses revised before sign-out yielded an overall AI Impact™ of 1.8%, ranging from 0.75% up to 3.5% per individual pathologist.
evidence.quote: In our real-world data, AI Impact™ ranged from 0.75% up to 3.5% per individual pathologist, with a normalized group effect of 1.8%.
evidence.sample_unit: cases (122,441 slides) in 3-year deployment; validation 101 cases/1279 slides

evidence.title: Implementation of an AI Algorithm in Clinical Practice to Reduce Missed Incidental Pulmonary Embolisms on Chest CT and Its Impact on Short-Term Survival
evidence.outcome: Radiologist missed iPE rate with AI in clinical workflow versus before AI
evidence.effect: Missed iPEs by radiologists fell from 50% (cohort 1) to 7.1% after AI implementation, P < 0.001; standalone AI sensitivity 90-95%, PPV 69-95%.
evidence.quote: The rate of missed iPEs by radiologists dropped to 7.1% after AI implementation, showing a significant improvement ( P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Use of natural language processing to identify patients with inflammatory breast cancer across a health-care system
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value with human-in-the-loop
evidence.effect: Initial NLP screening had a 55.4% positive predictive value, which improved to 78.4% when a human-in-the-loop review was added.
evidence.quote: Initial NLP screening achieved 55.4% positive predictive value, improving to 78.4% with human-in-the-loop review.

evidence.title: Closing the Performance Gap between Generalists and Breast Imaging Specialists Using a Nationally Deployed AI Workflow for Screening Mammography
evidence.outcome: Radiologist cancer detection rates before and after introduction of the AI workflow
evidence.effect: Generalists improved from 3.76 to 4.99 cancers per 1000 examinations (P < .001); specialists showed no significant change, from 4.47 to 4.76 (P = .33).
evidence.quote: Adjusted results show that the CDR of generalists increased from 3.76 (95% CI: 3.46, 4.08) to 4.99 (95% CI: 4.51, 5.53; P < .001) cancers per 1000 examinations with the AI workflow.

evidence.title: Quality assurance for deep learning-based proton therapy planning in routine clinical use for oropharyngeal cancer
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: clinical goal achievement
evidence.effect: increased from 91% to 93.6% in therapeutic volume and 78.2% to 88.5% in elective volume after manual adjustments
evidence.quote: Manual adjustments resulted in an increase of clinical goal achievement from 91% (sDLO, n = 71) to 93.6% (mDLO, n = 73) in CTV therapeutic and 78.2% (sDLO, n = 61) to 88.5% (mDLO, n = 69) in CTV elective ( Fig. 1 , Supplementary Table S4).

evidence.title: Verifiable Summarization of Electronic Health Records Using Large Language Models to Support Chart Review
evidence.outcome: Physician question-answering accuracy and completion time with vs without LLM summaries
evidence.effect: Accuracy 88.0% with summaries vs 86.4% without; overall completion time not significantly reduced, though frequent summary use significantly sped completion (p = 0.002).
evidence.quote: Importantly, summary use maintained accuracy in answering clinical questions (88.0% with summaries vs. 86.4% without).

evidence.title: AI-literacy training enhances physician-LLM diagnostic collaboration in a resource-limited setting: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Human-AI team diagnostic reasoning versus physicians alone and LLM alone
evidence.effect: Physician+LLM 71.4% vs 42.6% without LLM; LLM alone exceeded trained physicians by 11.5 pp; in 38% of cases physician+LLM surpassed median LLM-alone.
evidence.quote: While LLM alone outperformed the trained physician group by 11.5 percentage points (95% CI, 5.5 to 17.5; P < 0.001), in 38% of cases the physician plus LLM group surpassed the median LLM-alone performance, highlighting physician-AI complementarities.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-assisted reader evaluation in acute CT head interpretation (AI-REACT): a multireader multicase study
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in the reading workflow versus unaided, rather than standalone model metrics
evidence.effect: AI assistance raised pooled reader sensitivity from 82.8% to 89.7% but lowered specificity from 84.5% to 78.9%; reader confidence AUC did not change significantly.
evidence.quote: AI-assisted interpretation increased reader sensitivity for critical abnormalities but reduced specificity.
evidence.sample_unit: readers (each interpreting 150 NCCTH scans unaided and with AI)

evidence.title: OphAgent: A Generalisable Ophthalmic Agentic System for Global Eye Care
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance when using the AI in workflow versus without, in reader study
evidence.effect: Ophthalmologists' diagnostic accuracy improved by up to 20% across 14 tasks with OphAgent assistance.
evidence.quote: In a large-scale global reader study with 311 ophthalmologists from 86 centres across 22 countries, spanning seven languages and settings from tertiary hospitals to resource-limited clinics, OphAgent improved diagnostic accuracy by up to 20% across 14 clinically significant tasks.

evidence.title: Explainable AI as a Double-Edged Sword in Dermatology: The Impact on Clinicians versus The Public
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance of clinicians and lay users when assisted by AI and XAI versus unassisted
evidence.effect: AI assistance balanced across skin tones improved accuracy and reduced diagnostic disparities; effects varied by explanation type, expertise, and timing.
evidence.quote: AI assistance balanced across skin tones improved accuracy and reduced diagnostic disparities.

evidence.title: A foundation-model-powered AI system with post-read alerts and concurrent assistance improves gastric biopsy diagnosis across 29 pathological categories
evidence.outcome: Reader sensitivity for malignancy and metaplasia
evidence.effect: Sensitivity improved for malignancy 92.2% to 94.8%, P = .034; metaplasia 94.2% to 97.4%, P = .013.
evidence.quote: In a prospective reader study with six pathologists, concurrent AI assistance significantly improves sensitivity for malignancy (92.2% to 94.8%,  <italic>P</italic>  = .034) and metaplasia (94.2% to 97.4%,  <italic>P</italic>  = .013).
evidence.sample_unit: pathologists (reader study); 4,679 biopsies in retrospective multi-hospital simulation

evidence.title: Consensus, dissensus and synergy between clinicians and specialist foundation models in radiology report generation
evidence.outcome: clinician-AI report composition
evidence.effect: Synergistic improvement across all clinical settings; no numeric effect reported in abstract.
evidence.quote: For reports that contain errors we develop an assistive setting, the first demonstration of clinician-AI collaboration for radiology report composition, and we observe a synergistic improvement across all clinical settings.
evidence.sample_unit: certified radiologists evaluating AI-generated and human-written chest radiograph reports

evidence.title: Development and Testing of a Novel Large Language Model-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems for Medication Safety in 12 Clinical Specialties
evidence.outcome: standalone versus co-pilot performance
evidence.effect: Co-pilot mode optimized accuracy, recall, and F1; no numeric effect values reported in abstract.
evidence.quote: When employed in a co-pilot mode, accuracy, recall, and F1 scores were optimized, indicating effectiveness in identifying moderate to severe DRPs.
evidence.sample_unit: prescribing error scenarios embedded in 23 clinical vignettes

evidence.title: Boosting LLM-Assisted Diagnosis: 10-Minute LLM Tutorial Elevates Radiology Residents’ Performance in Brain MRI Interpretation
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with LLM assistance in intended workflow versus conventional search
evidence.effect: Residents with LLM assistance had higher accuracy (44.8% untrained, 62.5% after tutorial) than conventional internet search (32.2%).
evidence.quote: This was followed by the LLM-assisted workflow before the tutorial (44.8%; 39/87) and the conventional internet search workflow (32.2%; 28/87).

evidence.title: Optical Biopsy of Dysplasia in Barrett's Oesophagus Assisted by Artificial Intelligence
evidence.outcome: Clinician diagnostic performance with AI support versus without, compared with AI alone
evidence.effect: After cross-over, gastroenterologists with AI exceeded their own sensitivity (+24.45%, p=0.020) and accuracy (+13.33%, p=0.039) and outperformed the AI model alone on sensitivity (+12.89%, p=0.024).
evidence.quote: Additionally, they outperformed the sensitivity of the AI model alone (+12.89% (2.11–23.67), p = 0.024) ( Figure 4 D).

evidence.title: BiTNet: Hybrid deep convolutional model for ultrasound image analysis of human biliary tract and its applications
evidence.outcome: Clinician diagnostic accuracy and precision
evidence.effect: With BiTNet, mean accuracy/precision were 0.74/0.61 versus 0.50/0.46 without (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: The mean accuracy and precision of the participants with BiTNet as an assisting tool (0.74 and 0.61, respectively) are statistically higher than those of participants without the assisting tool (0.50 and 0.46, respectively (p<0.001)).

evidence.title: Quantitative assessment of myocardial fibrosis by digital image analysis: An adjunctive tool for pathologist "ground truth"
evidence.venue: Cardiovascular pathology : the official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Pathology
evidence.outcome: pathologist reproducibility with AI adjunct
evidence.effect: Pathologist-AI quantification was highly correlated (R2: 0.79; p < 0.001); AI knowledge significantly improved overall pathologist agreement.
evidence.quote: The knowledge of the automatic quantification significantly improved the overall pathologist´s agreement, which became unaffected by the degree of MF severity.

evidence.title: Can incorrect artificial intelligence (AI) results impact radiologists, and if so, what can we do about it? A multi-reader pilot study of lung cancer detection with chest radiography
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in workflow, including interface configuration effects
evidence.effect: Human-AI performance depended on AI presentation: box reduced FNs (33.0% to 20.7%); keep vs delete affected FPs (86.0% vs 80.5%, p=0.03).
evidence.quote: There was evidence that the way AI was implemented impacted radiologist performance.
evidence.sample_unit: radiologists (each reading 90 chest radiographs across 4 conditions)

evidence.title: Real-world validation of Artificial Intelligence-based Computed Tomography auto-contouring for prostate cancer radiotherapy planning
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: clinician contouring time
evidence.effect: Manual vs automatic+editing time: Obs 1 24 (±3.5) to 7 min (±3); Obs 2 17 (±2.5) to 3 min (±1.5), p < 0.01.
evidence.quote: As shown in the Supplementary material ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), the time for contouring (manual vs automatic + editing) was significantly reduced (p < 0.01) for both operators: for Obs 1 it was reduced from 24 (±3.5) to 7 min (±3) and for Obs 2 from 17 (±2.5) to 3 min (±1.5).

evidence.title: Reader bias in breast cancer screening related to cancer prevalence and artificial intelligence decision support-a reader study
evidence.outcome: Reader performance with AI in workflow versus standalone AI metrics
evidence.effect: With AI, reader sensitivity shifted toward AI operating point: sensitivity 75% vs 81% without AI, specificity 86% vs 67%; reading time fell 38%.
evidence.quote: The shift in study radiologist operating point caused by concurrent AI decision support demonstrates automation bias which is in line with the results of two recent publications [ 8 , 9 ].

evidence.title: Deep learning-based platform performs high detection sensitivity of intracranial aneurysms in 3D brain TOF-MRA: An external clinical validation study
evidence.outcome: Effect of AI on radiologist diagnostic performance versus standalone AI and unaided reading
evidence.effect: Radiologists' mean SE increased 11.40%, SP 1.86%, ACC 5.88%, balanced ACC 6.63%, F1 7.89%, Net Benefit 12.52%, Brier score fell 0.06 with AI assistance.
evidence.quote: Overall, radiologists' mean SE increased by 11.40 %, mean SP increased by 1.86 %, and mean ACC increased by 5.88 %, mean balanced ACC promoted by 6.63 %, mean F1 score grew by 7.89 %, and Net Benefit rose by 12.52 %, with a concurrent decrease in mean Brier score declined by 0.06.

evidence.title: Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Generated Vascular Severity Score Improved Plus Disease Diagnosis in Retinopathy of Prematurity
evidence.outcome: Clinician plus disease discrimination
evidence.quote: Additionally, a significant improvement in plus disease discrimination was achieved as measured by mean AUC (from 0.94 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.92-0.96] to 0.98 [95% CI, 0.96-0.99]; difference, 0.04 [95% CI, 0.01-0.06]) and AUPR (from 0.86 [95% CI, 0.81-0.90] to 0.95 [95% CI, 0.91-0.97]; difference, 0.09 [95% CI, 0.03-0.14]).

evidence.title: Potential of E-Learning Interventions and Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Contouring Skills in Radiotherapy: The ELAISA Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance using AI in intended workflow versus manual contouring
evidence.effect: Randomized comparison showed higher DSC vs expert consensus and lower time with AI-assisted contouring; outliers (DSC<0.4) 2.5% manual vs 0.2% AI-assisted.
evidence.quote: With an (arbitrary) threshold in DSC at 0.4, 2.5% of manual contours and only 0.2% of AI-assisted contours were outliers.
evidence.country: Multiple low- and middle-income countries (23 institutions, IAEA); cases from Denmark

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted delineation for postoperative radiotherapy in patients with lung cancer: a prospective, multi-center, cohort study
evidence.outcome: Performance of clinicians using AI in workflow versus standalone AI and manual delineation
evidence.effect: AI-assisted CTV had lower HD and MDA and higher DSC than comparators (DSC 0.745 vs 0.703, P<0.05); time shortened 43.2% for CTV and 56.2% for OARs.
evidence.quote: Our findings demonstrated that the implementation of AI-assisted technology could lead to significantly improved contouring accuracy, greater interobserver consistency, as well as considerable time savings.

evidence.title: Optimising the paradigms of human AI collaborative clinical coding
evidence.outcome: Human-AI team performance in intended interface versus AI standalone and human alone
evidence.effect: Senior-HITL reached recall 0.95 and precision 0.95; interns' collaborative results fell below AI-only ROC curve; seniors and juniors exceeded both human-only and AI-only setups.
evidence.quote: Overall, senior-HITL had the highest recall (0.95) and precision (0.95) with a small in-group variance.

evidence.title: AI-assisted radiologists vs. standard double reading for rib fracture detection on CT images: A real-world clinical study
evidence.outcome: Patient-level diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of AI-assisted radiologists versus standard double-reading
evidence.effect: AI-assisted sensitivity was 94.2% versus 69.2% for double-reading: increase 25.0% (95% CI: 10.5, 39.5; P < 0.001). Specificity was 100% versus 98.2%.
evidence.quote: The sensitivity at patient level was estimated at 94.2% in AI-assisted group and 69.2% in double-reading, with an increase estimated at 25.0% (95% CI: 10.5, 39.5; P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Safety of human-AI cooperative decision-making within intensive care: A physical simulation study
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in simulated intended workflow, including effect on decisions
evidence.effect: AI advice altered treatment decisions; 92% of unsafe recommendations stopped or escalated versus 29% of safe ones stopped, which standalone metrics would not reveal.
evidence.quote: The proportion stopping unsafe AI recommendations rose to 92 ± 3%, 95% CI: 0.86–0.98 (p = 0.0823) when including physicians who asked for a senior opinion, which would most likely lead to the unsafe AI recommendation being rejected (see Fig 3a ).

evidence.title: Improving the Real-Time Classification of Disease Severity in Ulcerative Colitis: Artificial Intelligence as the Trigger for a Second Opinion
evidence.outcome: user performance with AI
evidence.effect: AI support improved non-IBD experts' performance by 12%; disagreement with the primary physician was 20%-39% of cases.
evidence.quote: When used as a supporting system, it improved non-IBD experts' performance by 12% and disagreed with the primary physician in 20%-39% of cases.

evidence.title: Clinician-artificial intelligence collaboration: A win-win solution for efficiency and reliability in atrial fibrillation diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Human-AI diagnostic performance
evidence.effect: All patients were correctly identified, and clinicians' workload was reduced by 76.7%.
evidence.quote: After implementing the proposed clinician-AI collaboration strategy, all patients were correctly identified, and clinicians' workload was reduced by 76.7%.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence for Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening: Comparison of Utilization Scenarios
evidence.outcome: Reader performance with AI assistance in workflow versus without AI
evidence.effect: AI assistance raised recall rate to 30.3% from 22.1% and lowered specificity to 81.1% from 88.8%, with no sensitivity gain (64.8% vs 64.2%).
evidence.quote: Compared with interpretation without AI (recall rate, 22.1%; per-nodule sensitivity, 64.2%; per-examination specificity, 88.8%; mean interpretation time, 164 seconds), AI as an assistant showed higher recall rate (30.3%; p < .001), lower per-examination specificity (81.1%), and no significant change in per-nodule sensitivity (64.8%; p = .86) or mean interpretation time (161 seconds; p = .48)

evidence.title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
evidence.outcome: false negatives and false positives across workflows
evidence.effect: Radiologist 2.7% FN/1.2% FP; standalone 1.5%/6.8%; problem-solving 3.2%/0.6%; triage 2.1%/1.7%; safety-net 0.07%/7.6%.
evidence.quote: All AI-implementation methods changed overall FN and FP with statistical significance (p < 0.001): AI-standalone 1.5 % FN (23/1508; 11 consequences), 6.8 % FP (103/1508); AI-problem-solving 3.2 % FN (48/1508; 31 consequences), 0.6 % FP (9/1508); AI-triage 2.1 % FN (32/1508; 18 consequences), 1.7 % FP (26/1508); AI-safety net 0.07 % FN (1/1508; 1 consequence), 7.6 % FP (115/1508).

evidence.title: The impact of AI feedback on the accuracy of diagnosis, decision switching and trust in radiography
evidence.outcome: AI performance as used by clinicians, effect on user accuracy versus standalone model
evidence.effect: The AI was correct on 57.1% of exams, yet net user accuracy improved with AI feedback in most conditions; harmful when AI was incorrect.
evidence.quote: In most conditions there was a positive impact from the AI feedback despite the poor performance of the model.

evidence.title: Augmented reality microscopy to bridge trust between AI and pathologists
evidence.outcome: AI performance as used by pathologists in workflow (manual vs AI-assisted scoring agreement and positive calls)
evidence.effect: AI assistance increased ICC (e.g., total tumor cells 0.38 to 0.90) and positive CPS≥5 cases from 15 to 26 (31% increase).
evidence.quote: Pathologists identified 15 cases as PD-L1 CPS ≥ 5 positive with manual scoring on day 1 compared to 26 cases as PD-L1 CPS ≥ 5 positive by AI-assisted scoring on day 2, corresponding to a 31% increase of positive cases found when using AI-assistance.
evidence.sample_unit: pathologists scoring 35 biopsy regions of interest

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence algorithm improves radiologists' bone age assessment accuracy
evidence.venue: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association : JCMA
evidence.outcome: Effect of AI on radiologist performance in reader-study workflow versus standalone
evidence.effect: Radiologist MAD improved from 0.74 to 0.46 years with AI assistance (p<0.001); proportion >1 year error fell 24.0% to 8.4%.
evidence.quote: As illustrated in Fig. 5 , the radiologists’ assessment accuracy improved significantly ( p < 0.001) with AI assistance (MAD, 0.46 years) when compared with that without AI assistance (MAD, 0.74 years).

evidence.title: Enhancing the Accuracy of Human Phenotype Ontology Identification: Comparative Evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in workflow versus without AI and versus standalone model
evidence.effect: Physician+ChatGPT-4o accuracy 67.4% exceeded standalone ChatGPT-4o (48%) and manual searching (20.4%).
evidence.quote: Our study reveals that collaboration between junior physicians and ChatGPT-4o significantly enhances HPO description accuracy for rare diseases, outperforming both traditional methods and standalone MLLM use.
evidence.sample_unit: junior physicians (27 patient images each, 540 descriptions)

evidence.title: Empirically derived evaluation requirements for responsible deployments of AI in safety-critical settings
evidence.outcome: Joint nurse-AI performance versus AI standalone metrics in the intended interface
evidence.effect: Favorable standalone AI benchmarks did not ensure safe joint performance; AI augmentation both improved and degraded nurse performance depending on AI correctness.
evidence.quote: Due to these interactions, optimizing the performance of AI algorithms alone does not necessarily optimize the performance of the joint human-AI system 44 , 45 .
evidence.sample_unit: participants (450 nursing students and 12 licensed nurses; 4125 case records analyzed)

evidence.title: Comparison of Artificial Intelligence Models and Human Experts in Managing Dyslipidemia: Assessment of Adherence to Clinical Guidelines
evidence.outcome: Simulated LDL-C target attainment for AI alone, clinicians alone, and combined AI-professor workflow
evidence.effect: Simulated LDL-C target attainment 83% AI, 64% cardiology professors, and 92% for AI draft plus professor supervision (12 very high-risk patients).
evidence.quote: Of particular clinical significance, a combined workflow incorporating AI-generated draft recommendations with professor supervision yielded a simulated target attainment rate of 92%, exceeding the performance of any single respondent group and approaching the ideal clinical target of >90% guideline adherence.

evidence.title: Large language model as clinical decision support system augments medication safety in 16 clinical specialties
evidence.outcome: Performance of pharmacists using LLM-CDSS in workflow versus standalone LLM or pharmacist alone
evidence.effect: Co-pilot accuracy 61% vs human only 46%; serious errors caught 66% in co-pilot vs 52% by LLM alone.
evidence.quote: LLMs alone were capable of catching 52% of serious errors, while that improved with co-pilot mode to 66%.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated prescribing error scenarios (40 vignettes) reviewed by 6 pharmacists

evidence.title: Evaluation of a commercial deep-learning-based contouring software for CT-based gynecological brachytherapy
evidence.outcome: AI-assisted versus manual contouring time
evidence.effect: Median time was 14.8 minutes/patient manually versus 6.9 minutes/patient AI-assisted (p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: The median time to contour all organs for manual and AI-assisted approaches was 14.8 and 6.9 minutes/patient (p < 0.001), respectively.

evidence.title: Impact of AI on Breast Cancer Detection Rates in Mammography by Radiologists of Varying Experience Levels in Singapore: Preliminary Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Radiologist performance with AI in the intended workflow versus standalone AI performance
evidence.effect: Standalone AI AUROC 0.93 vs consultants 0.90 (P=.21). AI assistance improved resident AUROC and inter-reader agreement, mainly in dense breasts and less experienced readers.
evidence.quote: Diagnostic gains with AI were greatest in women with dense breasts and among less experienced radiologists.

evidence.title: Quantifying the impact of a computer-aided diagnostic score on the clinical diagnosis of functional seizures
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with the AI score in the intended workflow versus history alone
evidence.effect: Reference group accuracy rose from 41% to 60% (+19%) and near-highest group from 67% to 82% (+15%) with FSLS; other groups no net change.
evidence.quote: The group of average readers (Group 5) was able to understand the FSLS enough to improve their accuracy from 44% to 60%.

evidence.title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
evidence.outcome: AI performance as used by human reviewers versus standalone model accuracy
evidence.effect: Standalone LLM accuracy ranged 0.403-0.777, while human-AI collaboration under M2/M3 reached 0.633-0.900 and improved consistency of human judgments.
evidence.quote: LLMs (like DeepSeek V3 and Qwen-plus) cannot yet replace human RoB assessment but well-designed Human-AI collaboration can improve accuracy and reduce manual workload.
evidence.sample_unit: domain-level RCT risk-of-bias assessments (300 per domain across 7 domains; 60 per domain in human-AI collaboration round)

evidence.title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in intended reading workflow vs standalone model
evidence.effect: Experienced radiologists with AI outperformed DL-3DABUV alone (AUC 0.90 vs 0.82); novices reached parity with the AI (0.84-0.85 vs 0.82).
evidence.quote: Experienced radiologists achieved significantly better diagnostic performance in both second-reading and concurrent-reading modes compared with DL-3DABUV alone (all P<0.01 for AUC, sensitivity, and specificity; Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1 ).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

evidence.title: Prospective quantitative analysis of hyperparameter and input optimization in GPT-5: comparative contribution to radiologist performance in abdominal radiology
evidence.outcome: Clinician performance with AI assistance versus unassisted in the workflow, not standalone metrics
evidence.effect: Radiologists' accuracy improved with GPT-5 assistance (73%/71% to 87%/86% to 94%); differential Likert scores improved to 4.56 and 4.49; assisted juniors outperformed the abdominal radiologist on differentials.
evidence.quote: Using GPT-5 with the optimal settings further improved their accuracy to 94% (81/86; 95% CI: 88%–99%) ( P = 0.031, P = 0.028).

evidence.title: From tool to teammate in a randomized controlled trial of clinician-AI collaborative workflows for diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Human-AI team performance in intended workflow versus conventional resources and AI alone
evidence.effect: Both collaborative workflows improved clinician scores over conventional resources (85% and 82% vs 75%); the two workflows did not differ overall (p=0.22), and actionable-decision scores were 8.9% higher with AI first (p=0.026).
evidence.quote: Clinicians in the AI-as-first-opinion arm scored 8.9% better than the AI-as-second-opinion arm ( p = 0.026, 95% CI 1.1–16%).

evidence.title: External validation of a commercial AI system for pulmonary embolism detection on chest CTPA: a multicenter study
evidence.outcome: Radiologist performance with AI in intended workflow versus standalone AI metrics
evidence.effect: Standalone AI AUC 0.807-0.810 was below radiologists (0.888-0.914); combined reading reached 0.928-0.934, significantly above AI alone in all centers.
evidence.quote: DeLong test comparisons revealed statistically significant improvements in AUC for the combined approach compared to either AI-only or radiologist-only interpretation across all centers (P < 0.05 for all comparisons).

evidence.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Professional Expertise in Adapted Physical Activity Prescription for Orthopedic Rehabilitation
evidence.venue: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology
evidence.outcome: Quality of output from human-AI team (novice+AI) versus AI alone and expert
evidence.effect: Novice with AI support scored intermediate, partially closing the expertise gap; NAI higher than AI alone in most conditions (p<0.01) but not equal to EP.

commentary.bottom_line: Workflow studies of AI in clinical use often report results that differ from standalone model metrics, and human-AI teams sometimes perform better and sometimes worse than the model alone. No study tests whether requiring in-workflow evaluation before deployment changes purchasing decisions or patient outcomes, so the evidence supports the reasoning behind the practice more than the practice itself.

perspectives.view: Three randomized trials and many comparative deployment studies measured clinician performance with AI in routine work. Swedish screening sensitivity rose from 73.8% to 80.5%, while chest radiograph readers showed no accuracy gain. Certainty is low because these studies measure AI effects rather than the evaluation practice, and their designs and outcomes differ.

Standalone AI detected 95.8% of micrometastases, but AI-assisted pathologists reached 80.0%. Standalone fracture sensitivity was 93.5%, compared with 90.0% for AI-assisted radiologists. A wrong-eye injection occurred despite correct AI warnings. These cases suggest that failures can arise at the handoff between AI and clinician, which standalone testing may not reveal.

Geometric segmentation metrics correlated weakly with physician correction times for most organs, and silent alert simulations predicted postimplementation performance poorly. AI raised cancer detection among generalist radiologists but not specialists, and CADe gains shrank later in the day. These findings suggest that local workflow and user mix shape results.

AI shortened sonography exams and coding time, and cut musculoskeletal reading time from 34 seconds to about 21 to 25 seconds without changing accuracy. AI-assisted mammography added 4-6% reading workload, and an AI triage tool did not shorten transfer decisions. No study measured the staffing cost of conducting local workflow evaluation.

One pathology deployment in Puerto Rico reported a 1.8% diagnostic revision rate after AI second review, and one Hungarian screening study included rural sites. No workflow evaluation reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. As a result, the effect of AI on clinicians who serve these patients has not been measured.

In simulated studies, physicians using large language models scored 11.5 to 21.3 percentage points lower than the model alone and often left out useful AI recommendations. For patients, this suggests that a tool's published accuracy may not describe the care they receive from a clinician using it.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployment decisions or patient outcomes between sites that evaluated AI in their own workflow and sites that relied on vendor standalone metrics. Future studies should report how in-workflow results vary with user experience, fatigue, and patient population, and should measure what local evaluation costs.
commentary.underserved_note: One test focused on a racial and ethnic minority population in Puerto Rico and one included rural sites, but none reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no direct evidence that published human-AI team results apply to their clinicians and workflows.
